Eggs are incubated for an average of 60 days [ab = 60 days] under a constant nest temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a duration that aligns with the prolonged developmental periods typical of large procellariiform seabirds. Hatchlings emerge with a wet weight at birth of approximately 211 grams [Wwb = approximately 211 grams], a figure derived from the substantial egg size, which measures 10.3 centimeters in length and 7 centimeters in width. This neonatal mass represents a considerable maternal investment, reflecting the lipid-rich yolk required to sustain the altricial chick through its first days of life. Following hatching, chicks grow rapidly, fueled by regurgitated meals rich in fish oil and crustacean parts provided by both parents.

Fledging, or the achievement of sustained flight, occurs at 120 days after birth [tx = 120 days after birth], a developmental milestone that precedes full independence at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This entire growth phase unfolds under the elevated core body temperature typical of adult petrels, which averages 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. From that thermal baseline, a predictable sequence of life-history events follows, though the timing of each varies considerably. The onset of puberty, or the attainment of sexual maturity, is delayed relative to fledging and typically occurs at 360 days after birth [tp = 360 days after birth] at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This extended juvenile period is common among Procellariiformes and is thought to reflect the time required to master the complex foraging skills necessary for pelagic life, as well as to complete the full development of the flight musculature.

First reproduction is a notably deferred event in the life cycle of the Northern giant petrel. Under the metabolic conditions sustained by a body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], a breeding adult typically returns to its natal colony to initiate its first brood at 6 years after birth [tR = 6 years after birth]. This substantial delay between achieving sexual maturity and actually breeding is a hallmark of K-selected life histories, wherein individuals prioritize somatic growth and the accumulation of foraging experience over early reproductive output. Once a bird commences breeding, its reproductive rate is constrained; field observations indicate that a single egg is laid per nesting attempt, and successful pairs generally produce only one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year]. Each clutch therefore contains a single egg [N_R_i = Each clutch therefore contains a single egg], representing the maximum annual reproductive output for this species.

Adult body mass provides a further contrast to the considerable size of the egg-laying female. While the maximum adult body mass prior to fledging can reach as high as 5,400 grams [Wwi = 5,400 grams], mean adult mass in many populations is considerably lower, around 4.5 kilograms, reflecting the loss of fat reserves that occurs after independence and the onset of energetically expensive foraging. However, some recorded specimens from more southerly latitudes have been documented with an ultimate wet weight approaching 6,500 grams [Wwi = 6,500 grams] prior to fledging, indicating significant geographic variation in body size. This intraspecific variability is likely linked to the productivity of local waters and the availability of carrion, a key dietary component for this opportunistic predator and scavenger. Adults are robust birds with powerful bills capable of tearing flesh.

Longevity records for the closely related southern giant petrel, Macronectes giganteus, have been applied to its Northern congener, providing an estimate for the maximum lifespan of this species. Under the typical metabolic regime of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], the oldest documented individuals can reach an age of approximately 47 years [am = approximately 47 years], a lifespan that places them among the longer-lived seabirds. This extended longevity is consistent with a life-history strategy built on delayed maturation, low annual fecundity, and high adult survival rates. The species appears to experience very low natural mortality after the first few years of life, with senescence only becoming apparent in the final decade of the lifespan. Such a strategy is viable only in environments where adult survival is consistently high and where food resources, while patchy, are reliably available year-round.
